title: While the mind still works
hook: hurry, not only because death nears, but because understanding may fail first (Meditations 3.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of book two, life as a stranger's sojourn. Your line was a traveler's stay. What did you treat as borrowed, and care for? Day five hundred forty.

Watching a grandparent slowly lose their memory can bring a particular kind of sadness. The body is still here. The hands, the laugh, the way they hold a cup. But the person who could tell you the story, or give you the advice, or say the thing you were waiting to hear, is harder and harder to reach. Book three opens with a short note in the manuscripts, at Carnuntum, a fortress on the Danube. Then Marcus looks straight at that possibility for himself. This is a tender one. Today: while the mind still works.
screen: `THE BODY STILL HERE.` → `THE PERSON HARDER TO REACH.` → `WHILE THE MIND STILL WORKS.`

segments.voice: First, the usual reminder. Each day, Marcus says, life is spent, and less of it remains. We've heard that from him and from Seneca before. Second, the new worry. But there's something else to consider, he says. Even if a person lives longer, it isn't certain that the mind will stay able to understand things, to think about what's human and what's divine. Breathing, eating, imagining, wanting: those may carry on. What can go first is the power to use ourselves well: to see our duties clearly, to sort out appearances, to think something through. Third, so hurry. Therefore, he says, we must hurry. Not only because death comes closer every day, but because understanding may stop before life does. Fourth, how to hear that kindly. This isn't a judgment on anyone whose mind has changed with age or illness. A person's worth doesn't leave with their memory, and the people who care for them know it. Marcus is talking to himself, about timing. If there's something that needs a clear mind, don't assume the clear mind will always be there. The letter to your children. The hard conversation. The will. The forgiveness. Learning the thing you keep saying you'll learn. Even the conversations with the older people you love, while they can still tell you the story. Notice the shape of the urgency. It isn't panic. It's the same steady push we've met all year: today, not someday. Marcus adds one more reason to it. Not only while I live. While I can.
screen: `EACH DAY, LESS REMAINS.` · `THE MIND MAY GO FIRST.` · `SO HURRY.` · `WHAT NEEDS A CLEAR MIND, DO NOW.` · then, large: `WHILE I CAN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Notice that your mind is working right now: following words, holding a thought, choosing where to rest. Let that be a small wonder for a moment. Then think of one thing that needs this clear mind, something you've been putting off. A letter. A decision. A question for an older relative. Picture doing it this week, while you can. The bell holds the time.
While the mind still works. Marcus says hurry, not only because death nears, but because understanding may fail before life does. Today's word.
screen: `WHILE THE MIND STILL WORKS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: while I can. Do one thing today that needs a clear mind, the one you keep saving for later. Day five hundred forty.

howItsDone: Some readers take this entry as a push to stop postponing tasks that need clear thinking, such as important letters, plans and conversations with older relatives.

notes: Meditations 3.1 paraphrased: life wastes daily; if a man lives longer, it is uncertain whether the understanding will remain sufficient; in dotage, breathing, nutrition, imagination, appetite continue, but the power of using ourselves, fulfilling duties, separating appearances is extinguished first; so we must make haste, not only because nearer death daily, but because understanding ceases first. Confirm.
